extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, hazard classifiers, label preparers, and other regulated parties responsible for Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for implementing the revised OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (§1910.1200), including compliance timelines, classification criteria in Appendix A (e.g., acute toxicity, corrosive to the respiratory tract), labeling and SDS update obligations, and transition provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered compliance dates for substances and mixtures (paragraph (j))
rubrics_metrics.description: “chemical manufacturers, importers, and distributors evaluating substances are required to comply with all modified provisions of the HCS no later than 18 months after the effective date (paragraph (j)(2)(i)) and those entities evaluating mixtures must comply with all modified provisions no later than 36 months after the effective date (paragraph (j)(3)(i)).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA determined these extended dates will accommodate most implementation needs; the agency is not adopting additional tiers based on supply-chain role (e.g., staggered timelines) because that could create uneven protections. The final rule amends paragraph designations to accommodate related subparagraphs. Stakeholders are encouraged to phase changes into normal SDS/label update cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional six-month period for workplace labeling, program updates, and employee training
rubrics_metrics.description: “new paragraphs (j)(2)(ii) and (j)(3)(ii) require employers to update any alternative workplace labeling under paragraph (f)(6), update the hazard communication program required by paragraph (h)(1), and provide any additional employee training in accordance with paragraph (h)(3) for newly identified hazards no later than 24 months following the effective date for substances and 42 months following the effective date for mixtures.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides classifiers and employers an additional six months after the initial compliance date for substances/mixtures to make downstream programmatic changes and training related to newly identified physical or health hazards resulting from evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition compliance option allowing use of either standard (paragraph (j)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: “chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, and employers may comply with either §1910.1200 revised as of May 20, 2024, or the previous version of this standard, or both during the transition period.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No provisions revised in this final rule have an immediate compliance deadline on the effective date (i.e., 60 days after publication). This transition option is intended to provide regulatory flexibility during phase-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relabeling exception for products released for shipment (paragraph (f)(11) update)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is finalizing an update to paragraph (f)(11) which allows manufacturers, importers, and distributors to not relabel chemicals that have been released for shipment and are awaiting distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to reduce waste and unnecessary burden from relabeling existing stock; it is not an unlimited sell-through period but does reduce the need to dispose of existing label stock and eliminates relabeling for products already released for shipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of impurities, additives, and individual constituents in classification (A.0.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed note added from Rev. 7: “Where impurities, additives or individual constituents of a substance or mixture have been identified and are themselves classified, they should be taken into account during classification if they exceed the cut-off value/concentration limit for a given hazard class.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA finalized adding this note to clarify that manufacturers and importers must consider hazards of all classified components when classifying chemicals to ensure accurate classification and improved worker protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture classification sequence is mandatory (A.0.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA revised the introduction of paragraph A.0.4.1 to state that, except as provided in A.0.4.2, the process of mixture classification is based on the specified sequence of steps in A.0.4.1(a) through (c) and is mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The previously 'recommended' sequence is now required, ensuring classifiers follow the defined sequence when classifying mixtures unless an exception in A.0.4.2 applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'evaluating substances' and 'evaluating mixtures' (compliance scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA intends that the terms “evaluating substances” and “evaluating mixtures” include hazard evaluations and updates to classification, labeling, and SDSs required to comply with the revisions in this final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarification defines the scope of the compliance tasks to be completed by the stated deadlines (18/36 months) and informs which specific activities (hazard evaluation, classification, label/SDS updates) are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute toxicity definition revised to reference serious adverse health effects (i.e., lethality) and remain test-method neutral (A.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA revised A.1.1 to define “acute toxicity” as referring to serious adverse health effects (i.e., lethality) occurring after a single or short-term oral, dermal, or inhalation exposure to a substance or mixture, and removed specific timeframes to keep the HCS test-method neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explains ‘lethality’ here signals that acute toxicity classification endpoints are those used in toxicological tests (e.g., LD50/LC50) and does not imply non-lethal acute effects are unimportant — those are covered elsewhere in Appendix A. Removing explicit timeframes avoids tying definitions to specific test guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow use of alternative in vivo indicators (e.g., clinical signs) and alignment of ATE notation (A.1.2.1 & Table A.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA finalized language stating that while some in vivo methods determine LD50/LC50 values directly, other newer in vivo methods (e.g., using fewer animals) consider other indicators of acute toxicity, such as significant clinical signs of toxicity, which are used by reference to assign the hazard category. OSHA also revised Table A.1.1 to use the notation “ATE” in ranges to align with Rev. 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCS is test-method neutral; classifiers may use scientifically validated methods (including newer approaches that infer ATE from clinical signs). The table formatting change is a technical correction to express hazard category ranges accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider human data in a weight-of-evidence approach for acute toxicity (A.1.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA added text clarifying that “in cases where data from human experience (i.e., occupational data, data from accident databases, epidemiology studies, clinical reports) is also available, it should be considered in a weight of evidence approach consistent with the principles described in A.0.3.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human data should be included alongside animal data when evaluating acute toxicity to ensure classifications reflect available human experience; OSHA finalized this alignment with Rev. 7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and labeling for 'corrosive to the respiratory tract' (A.1.2.4 and subparagraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA added a new paragraph A.1.2.4 to require the classifier to consider whether the chemical is corrosive to the respiratory tract if data are available that indicate the mechanism of toxicity was corrosivity of the substance or mixture, and to clarify how the respiratory corrosion hazard should be communicated on labels and SDSs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA prescribes a tiered approach: (1) If data indicate corrosivity to the respiratory tract and the effect leads to lethality, the label must include the hazard statement “Corrosive to the respiratory tract” and the corrosion pictogram in addition to the appropriate acute toxicity pictogram and hazard statement(s). (2) If corrosivity to the respiratory tract is indicated but does not lead to lethality, classify under STOT single exposure (STOT-SE) and use the hazard statement “Corrosive to the respiratory tract if inhaled” (used instead of more general STOT-SE statements) and require the corrosion pictogram rather than the health pictogram. (3) If there are other target organ hazards, use the current STOT hazard statement and pictogram in addition to the respiratory corrosion statement/pictogram. (4) If no direct respiratory corrosivity data exist but the chemical is classified as skin corrosion/serious eye damage, the classifier must consider available data (including skin/eye data) to determine if the chemical may be corrosive to the respiratory tract; if so, the classifier must include the respiratory corrosion hazard statement and corrosion pictogram along with already required hazard statements/pictograms. OSHA will add notes to relevant Appendix C tables and anticipates providing additional guidance on this hazard statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to use weight-of-evidence and avoid one-study determinative approach
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA reaffirmed the hazard evaluation process goes beyond identifying a single study and relies on a complete evaluation of all available information rather than an across-the-board 'one-study' rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments requesting adoption of a single positive study rule were out of scope or rejected; OSHA prefers evaluative approaches that consider the totality of evidence when determining classifications to avoid inappropriate categorization and ensure robust communication to users.

rubrics_metrics.name: International alignment and coordination option
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA notes stakeholder requests to align compliance dates with other countries and observes Health Canada has published its update aligned with Rev. 7 (compliance date December 14, 2025). OSHA will work with Canada on timing concerns and notes chemical manufacturers may coordinate compliance with whichever country's compliance dates occur first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers have the option to coordinate their compliance timing with international partners (e.g., Canada) and OSHA will engage on cross-cutting implementation issues; this is an encouragement to reduce trade/friction impacts but does not change OSHA compliance dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance development and technical assistance for classifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA anticipates updating existing hazard communication guidance (e.g., Hazard Classification guidance, Document ID 0008) and developing new products to assist the regulated community with classification, especially for smaller companies and topics like incorporation of non-animal testing results and methods such as CATMoS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the HCS remains test-method neutral and does not name specific tools in the regulatory text, OSHA may include information about validated alternative methods in guidance products to help classifiers implement the rule consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement discretion and recommendation to coordinate across supply chain
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA recommends that manufacturers of mixtures and downstream clients who use their products for further processing and/or manufacture of other mixtures work together to ensure sufficient time to comply, and states that where particular circumstances warrant special consideration (e.g., a downstream user has not received necessary information despite best efforts), OSHA retains enforcement discretion to address those situations as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination is encouraged as a market/practical solution to information lag; OSHA may exercise discretion in enforcement in isolated cases where upstream information did not arrive despite reasonable efforts.
